newsitem.title: FRANCE: Report would retain French state's sway on justice.
newsitem.headline: Report would retain French state's sway on justice.

text.p: A report on judicial independence commissioned by the French president recommends more protection for the presumption of innocence but retaining controversial links between politicians and state prosecutors.

The report, excerpts of which were published in two French newspapers on Wednesday, fell short of expectations it would urge greater independence to prosecutors who control judges investigating political corruption.
The judges have been held back in the past by government interference.
Written over the last six months by a 21-member commission headed by Supreme Court President Pierre Truche, the report is due to be handed to President Jacques Chirac on Thursday.

Chirac asked for the report following widespread criticism that the previous right-wing government was actively interfering in justice affairs to block sleaze innvestigations targeting conservative politicians.
The new left-wing government has ordered that judges and prosecutors be allowed to pursue political corruption inquiries without interference from politicians.
But government officials have said they would await the Truche commission report before deciding on permanent reforms.
The report appeared to come down in the middle on the basic question of whether investigations should be completely isolated from interference or left under political control.

To protect the rights of suspects before they are brought to trial, it recommended leaving decisions on preventive detention to a panel rather than an investigating judge, a reform it predicted would reduce the number of prisoners held without trial.
It also urged that suspects be given access to defence lawyers as soon as they are taken into custody and that police interrogations be recorded to prevent forced confessions.
But the most controversial parts of the report concerned procedures for appointing prosecutors and investigating judges, and links between the Justice Ministry and prosecutors.
It would exclude the Justice Ministry and the president from having a formal voice in naming investigating and trial judges.
The report further recommended that prosecutors, who are now named by the government, be appointed by the Higher Magistrate's Council (CSM), which currently appoints judges.
It would, however, retain the right of the ministry and the president to propose candidates to the CSM.
And while it suggested banning the Justice Ministry from giving outright instructions to prosecutors, it would allow a "dialogue" between the two.

New Socialist Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou has promised that the justice system would be depoliticised, but the report could give the government an excuse to go back on its word and take less stringent measures.

Guigou was noncommittal about its recommendations on Wednesday, saying only that the report "seems to have some proposals generally in line with the government's ideas" and that she would give it more study before further comment.

The left-leaning Magistrates' Union praised the recommendations aimed at protecting the presumption of innocence but criticised the report as too vague to prevent the government from interfering in sensitive cases.
"The powers that be can do pretty much what they want to," said union president Jean-Pierre Boucher.
"It's hypocritical. Instructions will be called opinions but they will be interpreted in the same way. The hierarchical links we oppose will be maintained."
